Passive homes drastically reduce energy use and carbon emissions. In Chicago, passive building is being seen in single-family homes and also in a mixed-use development set to be the city's largest passive home project.</p><p><b>For example</b>: When storms pummeled northwest Indiana in August, Beverly Shores was without power for days; some in the region were powerless for weeks. Violeta Burokas' home was fully powered thanks to energy stored from her rooftop solar panels. Her property was built with triple-pane windows, an extra-thick layer of insulation and thicker walls. Extra energy in her home is stored in batteries. Her electricity bill last month was $37.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjdkiit-l-n/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>SMALL BUSINESS entries.title: White Sox set lineup for Game 1 of Wild Card series against Houston Astros
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – The White Sox have announced their lineup for Game 1 of their Wild Card Series against the Houston Astros, and it resembles manager Will Venable’s typical attack plan against right-handed starters.</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3864c910-bc2f-11f1-a4e3-df0308020bc1" start="1"><li>Sam Antonacci, LF</li><li>Kyle Teel, C</li><li>Miguel Vargas, 3B</li><li>Munetaka Murakami, 1B</li><li>Andrew Benintendi, DH</li><li>Tristan Peters, CF</li><li>Braden Montgomery, RF</li><li>Chase Meidroth, 2B</li><li>Colson Montgomery, SS</li></ol><p> SP Hagen Smith</p><p>Right-hander AJ Blubaugh will start things off for an Astros bullpen game, and the Sox have pushed their left-handed hitters to the top of the lineup in response, with the notable exception of Colson Montgomery.</p><p>For the first time in all of 2026, Montgomery is batting ninth. It’s surprising in the sense that Montgomery clocked 31 home runs as a 24-year-old in his first full season and is often lauded as a central member of the White Sox position player core. It’s also not surprising because Montgomery hit .099/.215/.210 in September with a 45.2% strikeout rate.</p><p>Smith is kicking off a bullpen game for the Sox pitching staff, and is unlikely to work beyond two-to-three innings at a maximum.</p>

entries.title: City Council raises debt threshold, setting stage for potential fourth veto from Mayor Johnson
entries.summary: <p>A defiant City Council tried Tuesday to wean Chicago off its historic addiction to debt, setting the stage for a potential fourth veto from Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>By a vote of 32 to 15, the City Council agreed to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/14/city-council-finance-committee-borrowing-threshold-marty-quinn" >require future borrowing</a> to be approved by a three-fifths vote. That’s 30 votes instead of the current threshold of 26 votes.</p><p>But the Council's support in favor of the reform championed by retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) fell short of the 34 votes that would be required to override a mayoral veto. That means Quinn’s political victory could be short-lived.</p><p>“The mayor does have a history of vetoing really good policy. He vetoed the hemp [ban]. He decided to choose dodgy storefronts over the safety of kids, so anything is possible,” Quinn said, acknowledging that 34 votes is “a reach.”</p><p>“The policy is solid. Having more eyes around debt is a good thing. Involving more alders in the vote total creates more attendance, which I’ve been after for the last five years."</p><p>Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) has argued that if 26 votes is “enough to pass any and every” other piece of legislation, it makes no sense to “allow a minority of members to effectively hold everybody hostage.”</p><p>Johnson has hinted strongly at another veto, arguing that Chicagoans “need us to move with expediency” to fill potholes, trim trees and repair or rebuild Chicago bridges that are crumbling because of “negligence over decades.”</p><p>But with 40% of Chicago’s operating budget gobbled up by pension and debt payments, Quinn isn’t he only one who has targeted the city’s mountain of debt.</p><p>The Civic Committee of the Commercial Club, one of Chicago’s most influential business groups, made debt issuance a focal point of its financial recommendations to the city. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/24/civic-committee-commercial-club-of-chicago-city-hall-financial-crisis-recommendations" >In a report released last week,</a> the group recommended that city debt “only be issued to pay for capital needs” and that savings generated by debt refinancing be used “over the life of the bond term” and never for “immediate budget relief.”</p><p>The committee also recommended that the city “adopt the goal of paying down 25% of debt within five years and 50% within ten years.”</p><p> </p><p>Under Johnson's stewardship, last year the city borrowed $449.3 million to bankroll large settlements and retroactive pay raises for Chicago firefighters that City Council members had been assured would be covered by money already set aside in the city budget.</p><p>And just last month, Johnson refinanced up to $525 million in city debt to erase an $85.1 million mid-year shortfall without employee layoffs and allowed to use what’s left of federal pandemic relief funds to help close the gap, if needed.</p><p>Those are the kinds of short-term fixes that the Council's 29-member opposition coalition has ruled out in the upcoming budget debate. </p><p>“One-time money must not paper over a permanent problem. Borrowing, refinancing, reserves and asset sales have no business underwriting operations,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/28/city-council-opposition-pre-election-budget-battle-mayor-brandon-johnson" >the group wrote in a letter</a> to the mayor this week.</p><p>Even if Johnson uses his fourth veto to block the higher threshold, Quinn said he will have made his point about the danger of borrowing more money and, increasingly, structuring the repayment schedule to postpone the day of reckoning. Last year, the Council almost blocked an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/18/830-million-bond-issue-city-borrowing-costs-backloaded-repayment-schedule" target="_blank" >$830 million general obligation bond issue</a> that included a back-loaded repayment schedule that raised the overall price tag to $2 billion. </p><p>“When you’re pushing debt down the road or you have too much debt, it has an adverse impact on our bond rating and we’re going to have to spend more money for what we borrow,” Quinn said Tuesday.</p><p>With the mayoral election less than five months away, Ervin has accused Johnson’s City Council opposition of having political motives.</p><p>Quinn denied that his motives were political, saying the measure is the next logical step toward a truly independent City Council.</p><p>“Utilizing a three-fifths vote as opposed to a simple majority allows more voices to be heard and counted," Quinn said. "This isn’t a new concept. A three-fifths vote is required in the Illinois General Assembly on all debt-related matters. It’s a smart and solid practice that, I believe, the city should also adopt.”</p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson has countered that raising the bar for issuing new city debt “isn’t a political thing. This is math.”</p><p>According to the Civic Federation, the city’s outstanding net debt rose by 32.8%, from $22 billion to $29.2 billion, between 2014 and 2023 — an amount driven by increased O’Hare Airport debt that was retired by airline revenue.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Kankakee forfeits Lincoln-Way West win due to ineligible player, placed on probation by IHSA
entries.summary: <p>Kankakee has forfeited a win against Lincoln-Way West on Sept. 18 for using an ineligible player. The Illinois High School Association placed the Kays on probation for the rest of the season.</p><p>The Kays, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/27/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >ranked No. 20 in the Super 25</a>, beat Lincoln-Way West 28-14 in the game. Kankakee AD Chris Pickett did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Lincoln-Way West and Kankakee are both 4-2 after the change. </p><p>“We recognize that eligibility mistakes can and do occur, and we appreciate Kankakee High School being forthcoming in not only reporting the violation but also presenting a plan to remedy this situation from occurring again in the future," IHSA Executive Director Craig Anderson said in a statement. "The school’s football program was also placed on probation by the IHSA for the remainder of the season. Probation does not deny the school or program any IHSA privileges, but it does set the expectation that any further violations could result in more serious consequences.”</p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Cubs playoff roster set for opening-round series vs. Padres
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO – The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ roster for their best-of-three series against the Padres is in.</p><p>The team is carrying a dozen pitchers:</p><p>– Javier Assad</p><p>– Matthew Boyd</p><p>– Aaron Civale</p><p>– Kevin Gausman</p><p>– Clay Holmes</p><p>– Shota Imanaga</p><p>– Daniel Palencia</p><p>– David Peterson</p><p>– Colin Rea</p><p>– Ryan Rolison</p><p>– Jacob Webb</p><p>– Ryan Zeferjahn</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell said both Gausman, the righty who’s been bothered by his left shoulder since making a diving tag play last week, and Imanaga, who threw 12 pitches in an inning of work Sunday, will pitch in the series, though it’s uncertain, at this point, how they will be deployed.</p><p>Counsell’s commitment to a staff full of “out-getters” without specific roles come playoff time shows in the large number of starters and multi-inning relievers on this list. They could be asked to pitch in their more traditional roles or to be used in more non-traditional situations, the nature of playoff pitching.</p><p>Veteran lefty reliever Caleb Thielbar was not included on the roster after finishing the regular season with a 4.68 ERA and 11 home runs allowed.</p><p>Right-hander Edward Cabrera, who was acquired in a high-profile offseason trade but struggled this season with injuries and underperformance, was also absent. He was placed on the Family Medical Emergency List last week.</p><p>The Cubs put 14 position players on their initial playoff roster:</p><p>– Miguel Amaya</p><p>– Gabriel Arias</p><p>– Alex Bregman</p><p>– Michael Busch</p><p>– Michael Conforto</p><p>– Ian Happ</p><p>– Nico Hoerner</p><p>– Carson Kelly</p><p>– Pete Crow-Armstrong</p><p>– Pedro Ramirez</p><p>– Matt Shaw</p><p>– Seiya Suzuki</p><p>– Dansby Swanson</p><p>– Tyrone Taylor</p><p>The Cubs were undecided Monday whether Bregman would play third base, weighing whether it’d be too risky to expose him to further dangers in the field after he suffered multiple facial fractures when a foul ball hit his face a little over a week ago.</p><p>Bregman’s potential limitation to serving as a designated hitter figures to explain why Arias, who appeared in only seven games for the Cubs during the regular season, was included as an additional infielder.</p><p>Boyd gets the start in Game 1 on Tuesday night, a 9 p.m. Central first pitch in Southern California.</p><p>Game 2 will also start at 9 p.m. Central on Wednesday night. The start time for Game 3 on Thursday, should it be necessary, will depend on how many of the other wild-card series make it past two games.</p>

entries.title: City Council signs off on $2.5B parking meter sale — after making it a little better
entries.summary: <p>Nearly 20 years ago, then-Mayor Richard M. Daley <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/chicago-parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-city-council-compromise-explainer" >struck a deal</a> that allowed him to avoid raising property taxes, but has come back to haunt him and Chicago ever since.</p><p>On Tuesday, the City Council took a vote that made that lopsided agreement a little less onerous for Chicago taxpayers.</p><p>The Council gave final approval to New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners’ $2.53 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters after Council leaders brokered a compromise to sweeten the sour deal for the city. The Council approved the deal by a 46-3 vote, with Alds. Byron Sigcho-Lopez, Jason Ervin and William Hall voting against it. </p><p>It calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing, 5% of net income going forward and 2% of the sale price if and when the meters are sold again before the deal ends in 2084.</p><p>The compromise, brokered without Mayor Brandon Johnson's input but with a strong assist from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/mayor-brandon-johnson-corporation-counsel-mary-richardson-lowry-resigns-renee-hatcher" >retiring Corporation Counsel Mary Richardson-Lowry,</a> also reduces costly compensation the city is required to pay for every space taken out of service.</p><p>Seven times a year, the city will be authorized to hold special events that take meters out of service for up to 10 hours without compensating Stonepeak. That’s up from the current threshold of six hours. Those so-called “true-up payments” cost the city nearly $174 million through 2025.</p><p>Stonepeak also announced that its subsidiary, Air Transport Services Group, reached an agreement to sell Omni Air International, an airline that has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. And it has agreed to explore creating entire nonmetered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations with charging revenues shared with the city.” </p><p>Tuesday’s vote ends months of controversy that only exacerbated the tension and distrust between Johnson and the Council.</p><p>When private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi wanted out after recouping their initial $1.15 billion investment twofold with 57 years to go on the deal, Johnson entered the competition without consulting the Council.</p><p>The mayor submitted four bids to take back the meters, topping out with a $3.2 billion bid that turned out to be hundreds of millions of dollars higher than the competition.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> reward, either financially or politically.</p><p>It would have required the city to pledge to siphon other major sources of revenue the city depends on “if parking habits shifted, alternative modes of transportation become more common” or if parking and commuting habits changed.</p><p>The City Council was kept in the dark and learned of Johnson’s multiple bids only after the city dropped out. Stonepeak then emerged as the winner with a $2.53 billion bid that was nearly $700 million below Johnson’s last and final offer.</p><p>The deal still needed Council approval. That gave Council leaders led by Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) and former Finance Chair Scott Waguespack (32nd), an opening to make the deal a little better.</p><p>“We delivered to all of Chicago a better deal than we delivered in 2008," Dowell said. "Nobody said this was the deal of the century… [But] this deal is 10 times better than the deal in 2008.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-060000" name="image-060000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d31645/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/79f4620/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b2d6f8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd) chats with a reporter before the start of a Chicago City Council meeting at City Hall, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b2d6f8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a8706e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b2d6f8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Pat Dowell chats with a reporter before the start of Tuesday’s City Council meeting, where she and other City Council members approved the transfer of ownership of the city’s parking meters to Stonepeak Partners, a New York investment firm. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This time, it was Johnson who was kept in the dark. Richardson-Lowry helped, but kept the negotiations in confidence and maintained a firewall between the Council and the mayor's office. Johnson was briefed only after the deal was done.</p><p>The Council's five-member negotiating team initially pegged the benefits at $376.2 million over the life of he deal. Downtown Ald. Bill Conway (34th), an investment banker, has called that number inflated — after Stonepeak deducts interest expenses and adds the potential for depreciation.</p><p>But almost anything would be better than the shortsighted deal Daley struck in 2008.</p><p>The $75 million up-front transfer fee will be used to chip away at the city’s $36 billion pile of unfunded pension liabilities.</p><p>Waguespack was one of only five alderpersons to vote against the original parking meter deal. He went into the latest negotiation believing the deal was “ironclad” and came out with changes he never thought were possible.</p><p>“When you go to buy a car, do you get the price that you want? No. The dealer says one thing. You say another and, at some point, you reach the middle point. And that’s what happened here,” said Waguespack. “Yes, we were given a bad deal in 2008. We tried to break it open and this is what we got: Five percent over the next 58 years.”</p><p></p><p> Ervin, alderperson of the 28th Ward favored his own eleventh-hour plan to to create a public infrastructure trust to take back the parking meters. He likened Tuesday’s roll call to the lightning-fast vote that sanctioned Daley’s decision to lease Chicago parking meters for 75 years — and forfeit decades of recurring parking meter revenues — tying the city's hands for decades.</p><p>"Every time we tried to close a street,” Chicago Parking Meters LLC said, “ 'Screw you. Pay me.’ And here we are again getting screwed,” Ervin said. “I still stand on the premise that we should take our streets back.”</p><p>In casting one of the three no votes Tuesday, Ervin said that the “irony is that some of the same things” that were said during that 2008 debate are being said now. Then and now, Ervin said, the city’s precarious financial condition was used as a reason to approve the deal.</p><p>“We chose to cower down and sell out for $75 million,” Ervin said. “History will judge us poorly.”</p><p></p><p>Hall, who voted against the deal, said African Americans have been left out of the $17 million in professional services contracts tied to Stonepeak’s acquisition of Chicago parking meters. “This is not the city we all were dreaming of,” Hall said. If the city is 27% Black, African American contractors should be “27% in the deal.” </p><p> Chicago Parking Meters LLC, a consortium that includes Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi, had threatened to take legal action against the city if the sale to Stonepeak was not approved.</p><p>That was apparently enough to convince City Council members who wanted nothing to do with the parking meter deal to cast a vote they hope won’t come back to haunt the city like it did with Daley, who compounded the problem by spending the $1.15 billion in proceeds while pension funds sunk deeper into a hole.</p>

entries.title: Even with QB Caleb Williams potentially returning, NFL moves Bears-Packers Week 5 game to noon kickoff
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>-Packers rivalry tends to be one of the NFL's biggest draws, but the league and Fox opted to move the Week 5 matchup out of the late-afternoon national window. The teams now will kick off at 12 p.m. at Lambeau Field after their game was flexed out in favor of Seahawks-49ers.</p><p>The Packers announced the change Tuesday.</p><p>Not only is that typically a coveted matchup for television, but it could be Bears quarterback Caleb Williams' return. Williams has been out since suffering a significant hamstring injury and is projected to be coming back around that game.</p><p>In the meantime, the Bears host the Jets on Sunday at 12 p.m. after upending the Eagles 27-7 on Monday night.</p><p>With Williams out all week and backup quarterback Tyson Bagent in the concussion protocol for most of it, the Bears started third-stringer Case Keenum. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/28/bears-inactives-vs-eagles-k-cairo-santos-cb-tyrique-stevenson-good-to-go" >He completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and two touchdowns for a 110.8 passer rating</a> and rushed for a touchdown. The Bears have not named a starter for Sunday.</p>

entries.title: Chicago cop charged with punching teenage girl during confrontation shown in viral video
entries.summary: <p>An embattled Chicago police sergeant was charged with punching a 17-year-old girl as she filmed a now-viral video that showed the cop threatening a group of kids this summer on the Southwest Side.</p><p>Jeremy Sikorski, 45, of Garfield Ridge, faces felony counts of aggravated battery in relation to the alleged attack Aug. 9 in the 5100 block of South Merrimac Avenue, according to Cook County court records. Sikorski turned himself over to police last week.</p><p>Sikorski and his family were attending a barbecue when Sikorski and two other men approached a group of teenagers in an alley, prosecutors said in a court filing. Prosecutors said the video shows Sikorski berating one of the teens about “picking on” other kids, apparently referencing an earlier fracas at a park that involved at least one of Sikorski’s children.</p><p>Sikorski then approached the teenage boy, first threatening to slap him and then warning that he would “knock your f------ a-- out” while raising a fist, prosecutors said, referencing the video. Sikorski also allegedly threatened to beat up the teen’s parents and menaced another person.</p><p>After Sikorski started to walk away, he turned back and punched the 17-year-old girl in her head, prosecutors said. Her phone fell to the ground and she was heard “sobbing in pain.”</p><p>Days later, she was diagnosed with a concussion, officials said. Prosecutors said she and five other people identified Sikorski as the assailant from a photo lineup.</p><p>Video of the incident was posted by CWB Chicago, a blog focused on crime and public safety issues.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">We have been informed that the man in this video is a Chicago police sergeant. <br><br>The name we have been given matches a known CPD sergeant, but we have not confirmed the identity, so we're withholding that info for now.<br><br>Details coming... <a href="https://t.co/tSkUgS1Svr">pic.twitter.com/tSkUgS1Svr</a></p>— CWBChicago (@CWBChicago) <a href="https://x.com/CWBChicago/status/2086920780172960196?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Sikorski’s attorney didn’t respond to a request for comment. An attorney for the girl’s family declined to comment.</p><p>The alleged attack was apparently spurred by an earlier altercation between the teenagers Sikorski confronted and a group of younger teens, described by prosecutors as the children of Sikorski and the host of the barbecue.</p><p>One of the older kids ultimately kicked one of the younger teens in the stomach, prosecutors said.</p><p>Sikorski later confronted the older teens in the alley of their home and asked if they were bullying the younger children, leading up to the attack, prosecutors said.</p><p>When police responded to a call of a battery, the mother of one of the older children told them the younger kids were the instigators of the conflict, prosecutors said.</p><p>Sikorski was stripped of his police powers two days later, police said. The Civilian Office of Police Accountability has opened an administrative investigation into the incident.</p><p>Sikorski surrendered at the Central District Sept. 22 to face charges, according to his arrest report. Prosecutors’ petition to have him held at Cook County Jail was denied during his first court hearing Sept. 23.</p><p><i>Contributing: Rosemary Sobol</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/21/chicago-police-cpd-vecchio-snelling" target="_blank" >Chicago cop with most misconduct complaints now charged with attacking woman as he faces firing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/25/chicago-police-alberto-rodriguez-crime" target="_blank" >Chicago cop with UFC aspirations faces firing over alleged sexual assaults of girlfriend</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/06/03/david-ross-larry-snelling-chicago-police-cpd-copa" target="_blank" >Chicago cop faces firing after passing test to join horseback unit while sidelined with ‘unbearable’ injury</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox finalize 26-man roster for Wild Card series in Houston
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – Ahead of Game 1 of their Wild Card series against the Astros, the White Sox released their 26-man roster for this round of the postseason.</p><p>While manager Will Venable loves to mix-and-match with different pieces, the actual roster contains few surprises. With a short, best-of-three series, the Sox went with 12 pitchers, allowing them to carry a full complement of platoon outfielders of either handedness.</p><h3>Right-handed pitchers</h3><p><b>Huáscar Brazobán, Sean Burke, Erick Fedde, Jordan Hicks, Davis Martin, David Sandlin and Grant Taylor</b></p><p>Though Venable said there will be no “bulk” pitcher used in Game 1, he did indicate that plenty of arms used as starters throughout the regular season could see action in short stints. In contrast, Sean Burke threw a traditional pre-start bullpen on Monday, as did Astros Game 2 starter Hunter Brown, so a more typical matchup of each team’s best rotation piece could take place on Wednesday.</p><p>The most notable exclusion here is middle reliever Trevor Richards, who logged 78 ⅔ IP in just five months on the team, but also threw 3 ⅓ innings in a save just on Sunday. Brazoban made the cut despite a rough early stint with the Sox after being acquired at the trade deadline, but Venable recently endorsed how he’s looked since returning from a left lat strain.</p><p>“He's working himself in a spot where there's that trust,” Venable said. “ The changeup was really good the last couple of outings. There was a 98, 99 in there with the sinker and four-seamer.”</p><p>The Sox haven’t commented yet on how they’ll use Sandlin in the postseason, but it’s clear his form while throwing six innings of one-run ball to help clinch a playoff spot in Kansas City opened some eyes.</p><p>“We had a big talk after the Kansas City start, and obviously conversations leading up to that,” pitching coach Zach Bove told the Sun-Times. “I told him [about] the progress [he’s] shown in that start compared to maybe one of the first starts of the year, specifically landing offspeed in the zone.”</p><h3>Left-handed pitchers</h3><p><b>Bryan Hudson, Anthony Kay, Sean Newcomb, Noah Schultz and Hagen Smith</b></p><p>Smith isn’t so much starting on Tuesday as he is opening up a bullpen game, and no one in this group of pitchers are likely to make a traditional start; certainly not in this round. Kay threw five innings on Sunday, but has been getting prepared for a relief role for a couple weeks now.</p><p>“They asked if I was willing to do it, and I said ‘Yeah,’” Kay said. “At this point you know you’ve got to be willing to do anything for the team, and if that's what it takes, that's what it takes.”</p><h3>Catchers</h3><p><b>Jake Rogers and Kyle Teel</b></p><p>Rogers is back on the roster after missing the final games of the season on paternity leave, but Teel should start every game.</p><h3>Infielders</h3><p><b>Luisangel Acuña, Chase Meidroth, Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas</b></p><p>Even with Montgomery’s protracted offensive struggles, the Sox infield is fairly static and Acuna’s biggest chance for impact is as a late-game pinch-runner. Chase Meidroth’s sore left hamstring kept him out against the Rockies, shifting Sam Antonacci to start at second base. Venable said Meidroth should play in the Wild Card series, though he is not quite 100% recovered.</p><h3>Outfielders</h3><p><b>Sam Antonacci, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk, Braden Montgomery, Tristan Peters and Tommy Pham.</b></p><p>White Sox outfielders operate almost like hockey players, shifting lines depending on the handedness of the opposing pitcher. Switch-hitter Braden Montgomery might ease this behavior in future years, but he’s produced better results left-handed and could be pinch-hit for against southpaws.</p><p>With the Astros throwing a bullpen game on Tuesday, and light on reliable left-handed options with reliever Steven Okert out due to injury, when and where Venable is enticed to deploy options like Grichuk and Pham before the arrival of closer Josh Hader into the game, will be a focus.</p>

entries.title: University of Chicago theoretical physicist honored as MacArthur Fellow
entries.summary: <p>When Vincenzo Vitelli fielded a call from an unknown number a few weeks ago, he exhibited extreme skepticism, believing it was a fraud or perhaps a joke orchestrated by a pal.</p><p>Vitelli, 48, a theoretical physicist and tenured professor at the University of Chicago, deals in mind-bending ideas every day, but the notion that he'd just won a MacArthur Fellowship and the $800,000 of no-strings-attached money that comes with it seemed beyond the pale. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.macfound.org/programs/awards/fellows/" target="_blank" >2026 Fellows</a> were announced by the foundation Tuesday. </p><p>"It took the people speaking on the other side of the phone quite a few minutes to convince me this was not a joke," he said.</p><p>The fellowship is an honor that is "intended to encourage people of outstanding talent to pursue their own creative, intellectual, and professional inclinations," according to the Chicago-based John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation.</p><p>Vitelli's <a class="Link" href="https://home.uchicago.edu/~vitelli/" target="_blank" >work centers on understanding the behavior</a> of information-processing agents — including humans, bots, cells and even individual molecules, which all possess the capacity for adaptive, intelligent behavior. </p><p>"Our research centers on a fundamental question: What laws govern complex systems composed of many such agents? What happens when you put them together and they start interacting? What is the emergent behavior? Can you describe them as if it was a material?"</p><p>Vitelli, who grew up in the historic town of Matera in southern Italy, said he'd like to use the fellowship money, which is paid out in equal quarterly installments over five years, to allow him to focus more on work.</p><p>"I'd like to use it to get even more freedom [on] the personal level, to intensify my push towards studying a less conventional form of physics," said Vitelli, who leads a team of about a dozen researchers. </p><p>A significant part of his work is simply inventing concepts.</p><p>"In part, my work is to imagine new materials and potentially even come up with ideas that change the notion of what a material actually is, blurring the lines of what people call materials, what people call machines, perhaps even what people call brains."</p><p>Vitelli says his mind can shift into imagination mode during his daily e-bike commute from his South Loop home to the University of Chicago's Hyde Park campus, at a concert or while taking in a play at one of Chicago's many theaters, or at home with his wife and 5-month-old son.</p><p>"It is something that can be somewhat irritating to the people around you who may observe lapses of attention on your part because your mind is flying somewhere else," he said.</p><p>Vitelli's concepts have undergone laboratory testing, but the research is still at the level of theoretical and has not resulted in any new technology or patents, he said.</p><p>When asked if he sometimes tells people he's an insurance salesman so he doesn't have to try explaining complex theories to laymen — like newspaper reporters — Vitelli said the opposite is more often true.</p><p>"Usually, if you say you're a theoretical physicist, you can achieve the same results more rapidly," he said with a laugh.</p><p>Vitelli has been a tenured physics professor at the University of Chicago since 2017. He earned his Ph.D. from Harvard University and came to Chicago from the Netherlands, where he worked as a professor at Leiden University.</p><p>"Chicago is a very vibrant city," he said. "I'm coming to appreciate it more and more."</p>

entries.title: Illinois environmental scientist wins prestigious ‘genius grant’
entries.summary: <p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and </i><a class="Link" href="http://grist.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Grist</i></a><i>, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p><p>Kaiyu Guan was in Singapore when his phone rang. The screen read "Spam Risk." He blocked the number.</p><p>He didn’t know the MacArthur Foundation was on the line.</p><p>“I’m pretty sure they called multiple times,” said Guan, 41, an environmental scientist and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.</p><p>The foundation came calling because of Guan’s groundbreaking work combining satellite observations, process models and machine learning to build resilient agricultural systems. The MacArthur Foundation eventually emailed him, requesting help with a “proposal.”</p><p>When they finally connected days later, he learned he’d won the prestigious MacArthur Fellowship. The so-called “genius grant” is awarded to 20 to 30 individuals each year, and it comes with a no-strings-attached prize of $800,000.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div MacArthur Foundation</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Some of Guan’s recent work has revolved around making regenerative agriculture easier to approach than ever before. Industrial agriculture relies on heavily tilling and plowing farm land, effectively turning over soil and releasing stored carbon into the atmosphere. Guan has collaborated on developing machine learning tools to help farmers take better stock of carbon released from their fields and perhaps how to better manage it .</p><p>His ambitions also stretch far beyond the Midwest which he calls home: “Monitor, model and optimize every farm on this planet,” Guan said.</p><p>Agriculture contributes <a class="Link" href="https://www.wri.org/insights/4-charts-explain-greenhouse-gas-emissions-countries-and-sectors" target="_blank" ><u>more than 12%</u></a> of global greenhouse gas emissions. Guan’s hope is that feeding billions doesn’t have to come with such a heavy toll on the environment and atmosphere.</p><p>Guan, bashful from his office, is grateful for the recognition this award comes with. But more than anything, he’s excited about bringing more attention to the world’s food systems.</p><p>“I don't want to make this about me,” Guan said. “I see this is a great opportunity for agriculture.”</p>

entries.title: Bulls rookie Dailyn Swain is a new man compared to his Summer League
entries.summary: <p>Caleb Wilson doesn’t just dabble in some light reading of the stoicism philosophy.</p><p>No, the Bulls rookie is all in, discussing it in length on Tuesday, and going in-depth on the ancient Greek and Roman school of thought that focuses on happiness and resilience by, according to Wilson, “controlling what you can control, and making sure that in every situation I’m kind of above it. I’m not going to let little things deter me because I know I have a higher purpose.”</p><p>This is really a 20-year-old NBA rookie?</p><p>It is.</p><p>So is Dailyn Swain. And a few months ago, the two first-round picks (Wilson No. 4 overall and Swain No. 15 overall) couldn’t have been in two very different places. While Wilson was the talk of Summer League in Las Vegas, Swain was letting “Sin City” swallow him up.</p><p>His four Summer League games were atrocious and even worse, Swain was carrying his dismal play from one game to the next. Vegas had him in its grips and wasn’t going to let go.</p><p>He left Summer League shooting 4-for-31 (12.9%) from the field, 0-for-7 from three-point range, and a turnover machine. The amount of time Wilson let his new teammate sulk in feelings?</p><p>Almost zero.</p><p>“Dailyn looks way better,” Wilson said after the first official team practice. “We were here (in Chicago right after Las Vegas). We’ve been here the whole summer. We’ve been grinding here. Seeing him every day, seeing him working on the things he needs to work on, me too, working on the things I need to work on.”</p><p>One rook pushing the other, and to eye-opening results.</p><p>“It’s night and day,” coach Tiago Splitter said of where Swain was now compared to Summer League. “It’s not even close. He was not himself in Summer League and I think we all understand that. He’s been great. He’s going through the little steps that he’s got to do and doing a good job.</p><p>“He’s producing for us, he’s getting into the paint. I think he lacked confidence in the Summer League but right now he’s a different player. He’s being aggressive, being himself, being the player he was in college.”</p><p>A statement being made by the Texas product.</p><p>“If you check his history everywhere he’s gone, he’s taken some time to get adjusted to a level, to the team he played on. It happened in college, we talked to his coaches, and he’s just going to take some time to adapt. Once he’s acclimated and confident he’s a different player and that’s what we expect.”</p><p>That’s also what they’re getting through the open gyms the last few weeks and now practicing starting.</p><p>“Just learning from it, taking what I could get from it,” Swain said when asked about not allowing Las Vegas define him. “It’s been easy to flip the page.”</p><p>With a little help from his philosophical fellow rookie.</p><p>“It shows what kind of kid Caleb is,” Swain said. “Everyone can speak to that. He’s a great kid on the court but off the court. We had no prior relationship, we met on draft night, and through Summer League we built a really strong bond. We go get food every day, and not just him but (two-way rookies) Tobe (Awaka) and (Jaylin) Sellers. All of them have done a good job with that. They weren’t going to let me dwell on it.”</p><p>Does that mean Swain has shown enough to be penciled into a rotation spot? No, Splitter isn’t anywhere near that commitment yet. But Swain does have his confidence back and he’s got a plan.</p><p>“I want to impact the game on defense, guard the best player,” Swain said. “The offense will come, but the main thing is being a stopper.”</p><p>And control what you can control.</p>

entries.title: Why Teuvo Teravainen is healthy scratch for Blackhawks' opening game
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — Teuvo Teravainen will enter the final year of his three-year contract with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> as a healthy scratch on opening night.</p><p>Hawks coach Jeff Blashill said he made the final decision late Monday regarding the lineup Tuesday against the Golden Knights, but things appeared to be trending this way throughout training camp.</p><p>"It's a hard decision because of the fact I think we have...more NHL players than we have spots to play [them] in," Blashill said. "I'm really not sure who's the best guy to go in tonight to win the hockey game. Tons of confidence in the guys that are in, but I have confidence if we had chosen Teravainen. </p><p>"He'll play on this trip at some point. He'll be a factor in our success this season, for sure. The hardest part, when you're in those shoes, is to maintain your own confidence, and that's not an easy thing. It's something he'll have to work through."</p><p>On Monday, Teravainen had a sense this was coming. He had been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/27/blackhawks-nhl-forwards-landon-slaggert-andrew-mangiapane-teuvo-teravainen" >rotating</a> with Andrew Mangiapane in line rushes.</p><p>"It's a little new for me, but I'll try to be positive," Teravainen said. "[The] coaches make the lineup."</p><p>The 32-year-old Finnish winger and member of the Hawks' 2015 Stanley Cup-winning roster had a strong return to Chicago in 2023-24, ranking third on the Hawks in scoring with 58 points.</p><p>It's partly a reflection of how much the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/28/blackhawks-lines-pairings-vegas-jeff-blashill-roman-kantserov" >Hawks’ lineup</a> has improved that Teravainen is now considered their 13th-best forward.</p><p>But it's partly a reaction to his struggles last season, too, as his production fell to 35 points and his play away from the puck suffered.</p><p><b>Situation to monitor</b></p><p>Confidence can sometimes be a roadblock for Teravainen. Blashill recently mentioned that when his confidence dips, "he tends to stand still with the puck more than anything else." Teravainen agreed with that criticism.</p><p>"If you feel good, you trust your legs a little bit more," Teravainen said. "And if you move your legs, you get a little more time to make some plays. </p><p>"It's a mix of everything. First of all, you need your head in the game to make quick decisions, be ready when you get the puck, [know] what you're going to do. And a lot of times, the first [thing to do] is move your legs. Everybody is pressuring so hard, so otherwise you don't have time."</p><p>His pending free agency next summer adds more intrigue to this situation. It will be something to monitor as the season gets underway.</p><p><b>Smith's quick return</b></p><p>Most Hawks players just endured an awfully long offseason. Fourth-line winger and penalty-killing specialist Cole Smith's offseason was a bit different.</p><p>Barely three months ago, Smith was competing for a Stanley Cup with the Knights, who he promptly faced as an opponent Tuesday.</p><p>"[Oliver Moore] goes, 'God, it's been a long time since we played,'" Smith said Monday. "I was like, 'It doesn't feel like it's been that long!'"</p><p>After the Cup Final, he had to take about three weeks off to let some small injuries incurred throughout the playoffs heal. Then, suddenly, August was right around the corner.</p><p>"You feel the pressure in the back of your mind like, 'We've got to get going here again,'" he said. "There's a weird balance to...find the motivation in the summer to get back training a little sooner than you probably wanted to."</p><p><b>Note: </b>Connor Bedard is traveling with the Hawks for the first two games of this road trip, although he's not cleared to skate with the team yet.</p>

entries.title: Un letrero de construcción anti Riot Fest aparece cerca de Douglass Park y refleja la frustración local
entries.summary: <p>Una señal de tránsito ubicada cerca de Douglass Park mostró mensajes contra Riot Fest el día en que originalmente se suponía que el parque sería limpiado y reabierto al público.</p><p>La pantalla digital estaba en el área con pasto en la cuadra 2900 al sur de Marshall Boulevard, justo al norte de Cermak Road y a unas cuantas cuadras al sur de donde el acceso al parque fue bloqueado con vallas mientras la limpieza se extendía hasta el martes.</p><p>El broche de la computadora que controlaba la señal estaba abierto, mientras eran visibles mensajes que decían: “Pro riot, anti fest” (pro disturbios, anti festival), “Gentrify GTFO Douglass” ([gentrificadores], fuera de Douglass) y “Go home Yankee” (vete a tu casa, yanqui).</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6f0000" name="module-6f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La señal es la más reciente manifestación de la frustración de los muchos residentes por la prolongada limpieza y las consecuencias del festival anual, que ha ocupado el parque durante casi una década y tiene contrato hasta 2027.</p><p>El Departamento de Transporte de Chicago (CDOT) explicó que la señal no era propiedad de la Ciudad. Riot Fest rechazó una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>En el <a class="Link" href="https://riotfest.org/park-impact/#access" target="_blank" >sitio web de Riot Fest,</a> el cronograma original de 2026 había fijado del 21 al 24 de septiembre para el retiro de la producción, la limpieza y la restauración, con el 25 de septiembre como fecha para reabrir el parque al público.</p><div Durante años se celebró en Humboldt Park, pero se vio obligado a cambiar de ubicación después de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/5/4/18556684/riot-fest-claims-damage-to-humboldt-park-repaired-preventive-measures-in-place" target="_blank" >quejas por daños similares</a> tras la edición de 2014 del festival.</p><p>Funcionarios del Distrito de Parques dijeron que generará entre $3 millones y $4.5 millones a lo largo del acuerdo de tres años mediante tarifas anuales de permiso, ya que el festival debe entregar una parte de la venta de boletos a la Ciudad.</p><p>Del dinero recaudado, el distrito de parques tiene una política de “devolución” del 30% para Douglass Park, lo que significa que entre $900,000 y $1.2 millones se asignan exclusivamente a mejoras para el terreno del vecindario de North Lawndale. entries.title: Out of the Darkness Walk raises awareness about the heartbreak of suicide
entries.summary: <p>Shaylin Takesue was smart and funny and beautiful, inside and out. In high school, she played volleyball, despite being 5-foot-1. She was a libero, the back row defensive player. At Illinois State University, where her little sister Olivia was also a student, Shaylin was busy and popular, interested in mental health. She had her own struggles, battling depression. Diagnosed with bipolar disorder, she sometimes spoke of suicide. But that seemed under control in the spring of 2023. Shaylin was out partying with her friends when, eight days before graduation, she abruptly killed herself at age 22, without planning or a note. Her sister found her body.</p><p>"It's hard," said her mother, Michelle Takesue, of Batavia. "You always think it's going to happen to somebody else. Not you. We spend our whole life as a parent trying to keep our kids safe. You love them more than anything in the world. You fear that something could happen to them, but you don't really get it until something does, something you pray never happens, the biggest heartache anyone could imagine."</p><p>Suicide is the second leading cause of death for Americans in their 20s. Impulsive suicides are common — <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11924695/" target="_blank" >one study </a>found that a quarter of those making serious suicide attempts consider the act for less than five minutes beforehand. Suicide can be seen as a kind of infectious disease — that's why journalists are asked not to describe the exact method of a specific suicide, so as not to inspire copycats.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e60000" name="module-e60000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>But comfort is also contagious. As is awareness. Both will be spread at the Out of the Darkness Chicagoland Walk Saturday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Montrose Harbor. Six thousand people whose lives are affected by suicide are expected to attend the walk, sponsored by the Illinois chapter of the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.</p><p>Sixty are representing Shaylin Takesue.</p><p>"We did the first one in Bloomington-Normal, right after she passed away," said her father, Tim Takesue. "To me, it was completely eye-opening. A little bit of healing, understanding that we are definitely not alone. To see how much this has affected people."</p><p>The walk is a blend of outdoor festival and somber commemoration, embodied by the "honor beads" participants wear — color-coded Mardi Gras strands: white for loss of a child, red for a spouse or partner, gold for a parent.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1c0000" name="image-1c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1c14a28/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5712x3206+0+539/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe8%2F34ba64ef4531a6fb84a0417dda03%2Fdarkness-4.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a9d9949/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5712x3206+0+539/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe8%2F34ba64ef4531a6fb84a0417dda03%2Fdarkness-4.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c7d5ab5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5712x3206+0+539/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe8%2F34ba64ef4531a6fb84a0417dda03%2Fdarkness-4.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Participants at last year's Out of the Darkness Chicagoland Walk to promote suicide prevention awareness. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c7d5ab5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5712x3206+0+539/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe8%2F34ba64ef4531a6fb84a0417dda03%2Fdarkness-4.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b98514e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5712x3206+0+539/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe8%2F34ba64ef4531a6fb84a0417dda03%2Fdarkness-4.jpeg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c7d5ab5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5712x3206+0+539/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fda%2Fe8%2F34ba64ef4531a6fb84a0417dda03%2Fdarkness-4.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Participants at last year’s Out of the Darkness Chicagoland Walk at Montrose Harbor to promote suicide prevention awareness. The annual event is sponsored by the Illinois chapter of the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.<br> </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"It's so simple, but it's one of the most meaningful activities at the event," said Angela Cummings, executive director of the Illinois chapter of the foundation. "They just look across the crowd and see all the people wearing beads. They lock eyes, and they know — they understand. Someone else is walking the path. It's so comforting for people to see others wearing their color of beads."</p><p>Purple means loss of a friend.</p><p>"That walk was very hard for all of us," said Melissa Blaber, who began a podcast, <a class="Link" href="https://www.blogger.com/blog/post/edit/3972382144120426476/3627536594124899727#" target="_blank" >“Stay and Slay,</a>" focused on mental health and suicide prevention with another of Shaylin's friends, Krissy Jerkatis. "The following year, we did our first Out of the Darkness walk in Chicago and raised $1,200 for suicide prevention. That was when we realized people do care about Shay's story. They're willing to help."</p><p>In 2022, the Illinois Department of Health started a three-digit phone number for mental health emergencies — 988. </p><p>"When people come to our Out of the Darkness Walks, they really get that sense of community. They get the strong understanding that they are not alone, and that help is available" said Cummings. "It does so much to reduce the stigma and get the conversations going, to have a giant event like this where every type of person comes out. You look around and think, 'Right. Mental health is just like physical health and it's OK to talk about it.' Just like any health condition, the more we talk about it, the more we treat it, the better the outcome."</p><p>But this is also a subject where good feeling can be fleeting, while pain rolls on.</p><p>"We are so beyond grateful and blessed at the people that are still supporting us," said Shaylin's mother, Michelle. "She truly is so deeply missed. It's like it just happened. That's the hardest thing to comprehend. It's been three years and feels like a month ago. I feel like I lost three years of my life. Three years I don't remember. It was an impulsive move [for Shaylin]. I do feel that in my heart, [her daughter's reaction would be] 'What the hell did I do? I didn't meant to do that mom.' That's what she's thinking. She was having a great night with her friends. It so terrible. We still can't comprehend it. What happened, this could not have happened."</p>

entries.title: Bears 3rd-string Case Keenum leaves no doubt he should start vs. Jets, even with Tyson Bagent healthy
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> third-string quarterback Case Keenum described his lights-out game in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/28/bears-inactives-vs-eagles-k-cairo-santos-cb-tyrique-stevenson-good-to-go" >their 27-7 win over the Eagles on Monday</a> as a dream, but also as a grueling challenge.</p><p>He thought of the 16-hour days, the head-to-toe aches his 38-year-old body would feel the next morning, and recalled telling his kids before kickoff that merely taking the field was an example of having the fortitude to “do hard things.”</p><p>And after everything he did to claim that victory, delivering a precise and prolific performance from the pocket, the question less than an hour after it ended was whether he could do it again.</p><p>“That's the best part of the NFL,” he said half-jokingly. “What's your reward for doing whatever it is on a night like this? You get to do it all again.”</p><p>That’s no certainty as coach Ben Johnson weighs the choice between Keenum or Tyson Bagent starting against the Jets on Sunday. Caleb Williams likely will be out again as he deals with a significant hamstring injury.</p><p>But there’s no denying what Keenum did Monday and no way Johnson can put him back on the bench.</p><p>He hedged Monday by repeating his line that Bagent earned the No. 2 spot over Keenum, as he did last season as well, “for a reason,” but also talked about how convincing Keenum’s week of practice was while Bagent was in the concussion protocol.</p><p>Bagent’s status factored into the decision, but Johnson felt fully confident in what he saw from Keenum on the practice field and behind the scenes “regardless of what was going on” with anyone else.</p><p>“There wasn't a whole lot of dialogue about it,” he said of the decision to start Keenum.</p><p>The Bears skipped the NFL’s standard day-after-game media availability for Johnson on Tuesday, and he did an interview with team broadcaster Jeff Joniak.</p><p>Joniak didn’t ask directly who would start against the Jets. He laughed as he told Johnson he’d get that question a lot in the next few days, and Johnson said only, “We’ll see how it plays out all week.”</p><p>It’s a time-sensitive choice in a short week. There’s little doubt Johnson will make up his mind before the Bears begin practice Wednesday because splitting reps would hinder the preparation of whichever player ends up starting.</p><p>This is a violent and often cruel sport, and it was brutal for Bagent to suffer a concussion the week before when he came in for Williams against the Vikings. In addition to the physical pain, it cost him the golden opportunity that Keenum received instead.</p><p>Bagent made the Bears’ roster in 2023 as an undrafted rookie out of Division II Shepherd, but hasn’t started a game since filling in briefly for Justin Fields that season. Williams had been remarkably durable and hadn’t missed a start until Monday.</p><p>Bagent worked tirelessly and quietly, winning over Johnson when he took over in 2025, and saw value in waiting patiently as he signed a two-year, $10 million contract extension last year rather than bypass it for the possibility of a much larger deal to vie for a starting job elsewhere.</p><p>Who knows what he would’ve earned himself if he’d played like Keenum on Monday?</p><p>But who knows if he can?</p><p>Keenum delivered an overwhelming argument to keep the job for another week, and whether that’s fair to Bagent isn’t part of the equation. All that matters is winning, and the Bears can’t overlook a Jets team that, while still early in a rebuild, has a decent defense.</p><p>Most teams hope their backup quarterback can do just enough to get by and avoid any devastating turnovers, but Keenum completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards with two touchdown passes for a 110.8 passer rating and rushed for a touchdown.</p><p>Bagent might very well be capable of meeting or exceeding that, but that’s hypothetical for now. Johnson has concrete proof Keenum can do it.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: How Bears' Dennis Allen used 'unique things' to dominate Eagles
entries.summary: <p>Only three <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive linemen were on the field when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/29/eagles-coach-nick-sirianni-remorse-for-screaming-at-bears-lb-dmarco-jackson-after-late-hit-on-jalen-hurts" target="_blank" >Eagles</a> lined up to go for it on fourth-and-five with 27 seconds in the third quarter Monday night. Linebackers T.J. Edwards and Devin Bush were bunched over the center, threatening to blitz. Behind them were a whopping six defensive backs.</p><p></p><p>The exotic look was vintage Dennis Allen. The Bears defensive coordinator had schemed all week to find ways to slow down the Eagles, who were one of the NFL’s best on third down.</p><p></p><p>Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts changed the play at the line of scrimmage. Edwards tried to listen in but joked he didn’t understand any verbiage left over from 2019-22, when he played for the Eagles. Hurts dropped back, threw left — and was intercepted by Edwards, who’d sunk into the left flat. It was the last of the Bears’ three takeaways in a 27-7 stunner against the Eagles.</p><p></p><p>“I think every week [Allen] has got some wrinkles in there that are going to try to show someone a different look,” said Edwards, who dropped an interception earlier on a similar drop coverage. “It’s for us to get to third and longer so we can get to those things. We weren’t able to do that ‘til we got to the second half.”</p><p></p><p>The Eagles converted 2-of-4 third downs in the first half — and went 0-for-5 in the second. They turned the ball over on downs on both their fourth-down plays in the second half, too.</p><p></p><p>Quarterback Case Keenum’s performance was the story of Monday night, but there was no more encouraging development than the play of the Bears’ defense. After giving up 37 points in Week 1, the Bears have now given up 16 over two weeks.</p><p></p><p>They got an assistant from a rainstorm and an opposing backup quarterback in Week 2, but Monday night was impressive. The Eagles went three-and-out on their first three drives of the second half, then threw the pick to Edwards, then turned it over on downs with about two minutes to play. They totaled 52 yards on 20 plays.</p><p></p><p>“I think it shoulda been a shutout,” said defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo, who had one of the Bears’ two sacks.</p><p></p><p>They were a split-second away. The Eagles’ only points came on a 1-yard quarterback sneak right before the second-quarter game clock went to zeroes.</p><p></p><p>Coach Ben Johnson gave Allen a game ball in the locker room.</p><p></p><p>“Putting us in position to make plays …” cornerback Jaylon Johnson said. “We had a good idea of what they liked to do and what defensive groups, what defensive plays would get us in the best position to make plays based on what they like to do.”</p><p></p><p>It looked different than it usually does. Allen went deep into his depth chart. Rookie Malik Muhammad started at outside cornerback for Tyrique Stevenson and never left the field. Five defensive backs played 70% of the time, including first-round rookie Dillon Thieneman, who had his first career interception. Safety Elijah Hicks played 22% of the time and Stevenson 8%.</p><p></p><p>“A couple of unique things in there this week that they really took to heart and did a great job with,” Ben Johnson said.</p><p></p><p>When the Bears led the NFL in takeaways last year, defensive backs coach Al Harris would pick a number before every game and challenge them to match it. Monday night, he wanted four.</p><p></p><p>He was undoubtedly thrilled with three. That matched their season-long total. With six — three interceptions and three fumble recoveries — the Bears trail only the Raiders and Panthers.</p><p></p><p>“The defense, the last two weeks, they’ve played outstanding football for us,” Ben Johnson said. “They continue to tread the right way. It's great to see the takeaways.”</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bellwood man charged in West Garfield Park stabbing
entries.summary: <p>A Bellwood man is facing attempted murder charges for allegedly stabbing a 28-year-old man in West Garfield Park earlier this year, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Shawn Jackson, 56, faces a felony charge of attempted first-degree murder, aggravated battery causing great bodily harm and aggravated battery using a deadly weapon, in addition to a warrant being executed, police said. He was arrested Monday.</p><p>Jackson is accused of stabbing the man in the 600 block of South Pulaski Road on May 1, police said. The victim was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital and listed in serious condition at the time.</p><p>Jackson is due in court for a detention hearing Wednesday.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: White Sox fans are 'all in' on long postseason run after 100-loss seasons
entries.summary: <p>Eager White Sox fans gathered at a South Side bar Tuesday in anticipation of the team’s first playoff game in five years.</p><p>“I am absolutely sick to my stomach right now, but in a good way,” said Patrick Ramos, gearing up to watch the Sox take on the Houston Astros in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with his brother and friends at Cork & Kerry at The Park in Armour Square.</p><p>Right now, Sox fandom is defined by a few things. Rookie slugger Munetaka Murakami (the “South Side Samurai"). Young, fun-loving players who show their personalities on and off the field. All part of an odds-defying turnaround from the dark days of 2024, when the Sox set a major league record by losing 121 games, and ticket prices dropped to $1.</p><p>Sox fans anticipate a win and hope to welcome playoff baseball back to the South Side. All three wild-card games are in Houston; the Sox must advance to the next round to play on their home turf.</p><p>“I can't wait for the crowd to be just as insane as when we were going to the World Series, as when we had the blackout game,” said Chris Ramos, Patrick Ramos’ brother. “I expect that level of intensity in that part when we come back after we win this series.”</p><p>And perhaps the team’s most famous fan is hoping for a successful postseason. Pope Leo XIV, a lifelong Sox fan, penned a letter to the team. It arrived at Rate Field this week.</p><p>“As I have noted, ‘sport can truly become a school of life, where all can learn that abundance does not come from victory at any cost, but from sharing, from respecting others and from the joy of walking together.’ In this spirit, it is my hope that the White Sox will continue to foster bonds of friendship and solidarity among people, and thus bear hopeful witness to the possibility of living and working together in peace,” the pope wrote. “With these sentiments, I willingly invoke the Almighty’s abundant blessings upon you and your loved ones.”</p><div </div><p>Glenn Kubek, 31, grew up in the East Side neighborhood and remembers meticulously following the Sox throughout his childhood — even watching playoff games while battling food poisoning during the 2005 World Series championship run. Now a baseball coach at De La Salle Institute, just three blocks from Rate Field, he said fandom takes on a different form.</p><p>“Growing up, we were so intent on baseball,” Kubek said. “I feel like the (younger) ages now in baseball don't watch whole games. They like watching highlights. A lot of kids don’t have favorite teams. A lot of kids just have favorite players or stuff like that, so it became a little different scene.”</p><p>Kubek and Rich Barnotes, 34, who also coaches at De La Salle, applauded the Sox coaching staff for its ability to put together a winning roster after three straight 100-loss seasons.</p><p>“To think when we were there in April of 2024, and you can hear the center fielder saying, ‘I got it’ on a fly ball, and now there's 37,000 people there on Saturday night,” Barnotes said. “It’s just a complete 180 turnaround.”</p><p>And for some longtime fans, the seasons spent suffering make a hope-filled playoff appearance that much sweeter.</p><p>“We were still here throughout the dark days, 100-loss seasons, and, you know, we knew it was going to get better,” said longtime fan Jason James. “Did we think it was going to be this quickly? Probably not. But now we're just going to be riding the vibes on this because we honestly, for all the misery that we've suffered, we deserve this.”</p><p> </p><p></p><p></p><p> </p><div class="Enhancement"
