entries.title: Reviewing Sky center Kamilla Cardoso's development
entries.summary: <p>It’s a bit mind-bending to consider, but center Kamilla Cardoso is one of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> elder statesmen.</p><p>Not in age of course — she’s still only 25, her brain having just arrived at full development — but in consecutive tenure.</p><p>Cardoso was drafted No. 3 in 2024, the Sky’s first lottery pick in many years, and is one of only two remaining players from that team. The roster, coaching staff and even practice locations all have turned over.</p><p>This season was her third, often an inflection point for young players. For Cardoso, people predicted it would go one of two ways: She would become an All-Star and dominate, the way she did her in senior year at South Carolina, or she would regress and reveal that the Sky were way too high on her with the third pick.</p><p>Cardoso didn’t exactly vindicate either view. Her statistics ticked up to a dependable 14.7 points, 8.6 rebounds and 1.5 blocks, but she didn’t patch up some basic aspects to her game other top centers have.</p><p>Is another leap still possible for Cardoso in Year 4, or have we seen what she is: a very good, but not quite All-Star level, center?</p><p>Coach Tyler Marsh is the king of reminding everyone that growth isn’t a linear process, which is reason to hold out hope. But part of the question is whether Marsh has the ability to guide Cardoso through it.</p><p>In her exit interview last week, Cardoso acknowledged her defense ‘‘wasn’t great’’ this season and needs to get better.</p><p>She has a couple of things to fix on that side of the ball. One is keeping a lower center of gravity in the post, so she’s not caught out of position. The other is keeping her hands straight up when she contests shots, so that she doesn’t foul.</p><p>It’s a little concerning that Marsh and his staff have allowed these habits to persist this long, especially given that Cardoso is the Sky’s best hope at rim protection and these are pretty basic skills.</p><p>Offensively, however, Cardoso has to own some of the holes in her game. Despite her solid shooting form and the coaching staff encouraging her to let it fly, she took only 10 jump shots this season. That’s even fewer than she took last season.</p><p>‘‘People have high expectations for me,’’ Cardoso said in her exit interview. ‘‘They know I’m capable of shooting the ball, so shooting the ball on the perimeter [is an offseason goal].’’</p><p>This offseason, Cardoso will head to Project B, a new 5-on-5 touring league that has so far announced stops in Valencia, Spain, and Tokyo. The league appealed to Cardoso because of the ability to travel, which she enjoys, and to play against elite competition.</p><p>In the WBCA Chinese league, in which she played the last two offseasons, Cardoso dominated against a lower field of competition. This time around, she’ll be able to compete against two of the WNBA’s best centers in Jonquel Jones and Brionna Jones. Both have the kind of footwork, finesse and physicality that Cardoso is aiming toward.</p><p>In his own exit interview, Marsh sounded pleased that Cardoso is going to stay in Chicago to train until Project B starts, giving him some hands-on time with her.</p><p>To that end, it would be nice if the Sky met their deadline for their new practice facility before Cardoso heads abroad in January. Management’s most recent projection was November, but if the Bedford Park project gets delayed again, it might mean another round of workouts in college gyms for Cardoso.</p><p>It’s also possible she will find herself working out with another round of coaches. The Sky still haven’t indicated whether they’re bringing Marsh back for a third season.</p><p>Given all the surrounding unsteadiness, Cardoso earned some credit for the player she already has become, regardless of whether the Year 4 leap materializes.</p><p>She might be the most stable thing the Sky have going for them.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: After work to build, guide Cubs, October is where legacies will be made for Jed Hoyer, Craig Counsell
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — Judgment day is here.</p><p>Judgment week, maybe?</p><p>Or how about judgment month? The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>, indeed, would prefer the latter.</p><p>This is the big time — the only time that matters — for the Cubs and their brain trust of team president Jed Hoyer and manager Craig Counsell.</p><p>October is where legacies are made.</p><p>The Cubs started what they hope is a lengthy playoff journey Tuesday in California, the ultimate test of what’s been built over the last several years.</p><p>MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong said last week that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/24/cubs-clinch-mlb-postseason-playoffs-pete-crow-armstrong-matthew-boyd-nl-wild-card-standings-red-sox-doubleheader" >this team was “built for the weird s--t.”</a></p><p>That they’re still standing after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-alex-bregman-face-injury-return-matt-shaw-bunt-daniel-palencia-stats" >foul balls to the face</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-magic-number-playoffs-clinch-nl-wild-card-standings-kevin-gausman-shoulder-injury" >banged-up shoulders</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-game-moved-boston-weather-fenway-park-tampa-bay-florida-tropicana-field" >weather-caused scheduling chaos</a> is certainly something.</p><p>But more than being “built for the weird s--t,” these Cubs were built to win it all.</p><p>Will they stay standing long enough to do that?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7Y62_NnBZwo?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="The Sun-Times' Vinnie Duber and Steve Greenberg preview the Cubs-Padres wild card series"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Hoyer has spent the last year making the necessary moves and smashing narratives about free-agent spending and clinging to prospects.</p><p>He handed out big-money extensions to Crow-Armstrong and second baseman Nico Hoerner. He gave $175 million to Bregman, who has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/21/cubs-alex-bregman-playoffs-stats-world-series-dansby-swanson-carson-kelly-craig-counsell" >proven worth the expenditure</a>, shaking off a slow start to become his team’s second best hitter and a tough, inspirational leader.</p><p>On the trade front, right-hander Edward Cabrera had bad days, bad blisters and a bad hamstring, not the top-of-the-rotation arm he was supposed to be.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >Getting aggressive at the trade deadline</a> to land righties Gausman and Clay Holmes seemed a home run, though their late-season performances — and Gausman’s nagging shoulder — have thrown into question how much they’ll deliver in the postseason.</p><p>But the moves were what they needed to be to craft a championship contender.</p><p>The Cubs aren’t favored to reach October’s end, not after once more <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/09/cubs-kevin-gausman-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-brewers-starting-rotation-playoff-starter-clay-holmes-ian-happ-phil-maton" >getting left in the Brewers’ dust</a> in the NL Central, which casts a spotlight on Hoyer’s most consequential move: poaching Counsell from the division-dominating rivals three years ago.</p><p>Counsell gets rave reviews from players and was recently credited by Crow-Armstrong with helping him evolve into the player he is today, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/21/cubs-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoffs-seeding-padrres-phillies-pete-crow-armstrong-40-40" >someone who can make a greater impact</a> on a game, a series and this postseason than maybe any other player in the sport.</p><p>During a roller-coaster season — the Cubs like to cite two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak to illustrate the ups and downs — Counsell steered the team through an avalanche of pitching injuries that threatened to bury it. At one point, the Cubs had an entire rotation and back-end bullpen group on the IL at the same time, yet they survived.</p><p>“He’s had a lot to deal with, obviously, starting from a pretty early point in the year,” Crow-Armstrong said Monday. “A manager’s job is how many different kinds of skills you have to have. That’s not necessarily making decisions in the game or anything like that. It’s about continuing to get to know people, continuing to build trust.</p><p>“He’s obviously battle-tested, and he’s had so much different experience through the game of baseball, as a player and a manager. We all just trust him, and that definitely seeps into how we trust each other.”</p><p>But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/16/cubs-second-half-preview-brewers-nl-central-standings-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-alex-bregman" >merely surviving was never the intended outcome</a>, and Hoyer’s move to land Counsell in the first place was made with only one goal in mind: getting the Cubs another World Series trophy.</p><p>What will become of their legacies this postseason?</p><p>Will they achieve their ultimate goal, hoisting a trophy that validates it all and dials up another championship party in Grant Park that shoots Hoyer and Counsell into the same stratosphere Theo Epstein and Joe Maddon reached a decade ago?</p><p>Or will they leave us asking whether these Cubs can ever get back to that place, whether they can do better than wild-card berths, and wondering how many more chances Hoyer and Counsell — both under contract beyond this season — get to turn in a better finish in the results-oriented, high-expectations business of baseball?</p><p>And so, welcome to judgment day. Week. Month. Whatever.</p><p>Both men have done impressive work in getting the Cubs to this place, but simply getting here was never the end goal.</p><p>This is where we find out if that work was enough.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: DePaul basketball coach Chris Holtmann agrees to contract extension through 2030-31 season
entries.summary: <p>DePaul coach Chris Holtmann has agreed to a contract extension that runs through the 2030-31 season.</p><p>Athletic director DeWayne Peevy announced the deal on Tuesday.</p><p>"This extension reflects both what Chris has already accomplished and our confidence in where he is taking this program," Peevy said in a release. "In two seasons, he has rebuilt the competitive foundation of DePaul men's basketball, restored belief in the program and elevated our visibility locally and nationally."</p><p>Holtmann was hired by DePaul in March 2024 after the Blue Demons went 3-29 overall and 0-20 in Big East play. He replaced Tony Stubblefield, who was fired after two-plus seasons.</p><p>DePaul went 14-20 overall and 4-16 in the Big East in Holtmann's first year in charge. The Blue Demons improved to 16-16 last season, including an 8-12 conference record.</p><p>"These first two years have been filled with both challenges and really exciting moments as we fight to rebuild this program," Holtmann said in the school's release. "We know continuing to move this forward won't be easy, but we embrace the challenges ahead. Our family has really enjoyed Chicago and we love our fans and the DePaul community, as well as the mission of DePaul."</p><p>Holtmann, who turns 55 in November, is 281-207 in 15 seasons, also coaching at Gardner-Webb, Butler and Ohio State.</p>

entries.title: Portage Park woman charged with stealing dead mother's Social Security benefits
entries.summary: <p>A woman accused of hiding her mother’s body in a freezer while she collected her Social Security benefits is among <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndil/pr/dojs-fraud-division-uncovers-134m-stolen-social-security-benefits-one-month-takedown" target="_blank" >17 defendants from across the country</a> who were accused of defrauding the program of up to $1.3 million, according to the U.S. Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division.</p><p>Eva Bratcher, 72, was charged in the Northern District of Illinois in August with theft of government property and fraud related to misrepresentation or misuse of Social Security benefits totaling $21,402. She faces up to five years in prison.</p><p>“The Social Security Administration’s benefits programs are meant to safeguard America’s elderly and most vulnerable — not to bankroll fraudsters,” Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald said in a statement. “Every dollar stolen is a dollar taken from a retiree’s medicine, meals, or housing.”</p><p>The charges come nearly three years after Bratcher pleaded guilty to concealing her mother’s death and possessing a fraudulent ID card, according to court records. She was sentenced to 18 months in prison.</p><p>Bratcher was arrested in January 2023 after police conducted a well-being check called in by her daughter, and officers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2023/1/31/23579316/body-of-96-year-old-woman-found-in-freezer-in-portage-park" target="_blank" ><u>found the body of 96-year-old Regina Michalski</u></a> in their 5500 block of West Melrose Street home.</p><p>Michalski’s body had been stored by Bratcher in a freezer in the home's garage for two years after she died in 2021. During that time, she is alleged to have collected the woman's Social Security and SNAP benefits.</p><p>A receipt found in the home showed Bratcher had purchased the freezer a week after her mother died. Bratcher is also alleged to have used another Social Security number to receive even more fraudulent SNAP benefits, according to prosecutors. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div She was sentenced to concurrent two-year probation terms, which she later pleaded guilty to violating the terms of her release before being sentenced to concurrent two-year prison terms minus time served.</p><p>Bratcher was also sentenced to four years in prison in 2010 for committing forgery in Lake County. She has faced a range of charges that were previously dropped, including battery, assault, retail theft, criminal damage to property, and reckless and disorderly conduct.</p><p>She is expected to appear in federal court Thursday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/2/2/23583052/woman-hid-96-year-old-mothers-body-in-freezer-for-nearly-2-years-prosecutors" >Woman hid 96-year-old mother’s body in freezer for nearly 2 years: prosecutors</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2023/1/31/23579316/body-of-96-year-old-woman-found-in-freezer-in-portage-park" >‘She didn’t deserve to go that way.’ Body of 96-year-old woman found in freezer in Portage Park</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/2/1/23581419/woman-charged-concealing-death-mother-body-found-freezer-portage-park-home" >Woman charged with concealing death of mother, whose body was found in freezer at their Portage Park home</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Ahora es casi imposible obtener asilo en la corte de inmigración de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Un venezolano creía que su solicitud de asilo cumplía con todos los requisitos para poder quedarse en Estados Unidos.</p><p>Tenía pruebas de lo gravemente que la policía local lo maltrató cuando lo secuestraron y lo sodomizaron, el punto más bajo de meses de acoso. Como hombre gay, se le considera parte de una clase protegida. Y después de que denunció las agresiones, los agentes juraron vengarse.</p><p>“Me van a matar, estos policías”, testificó en agosto. “Ellos sabrán cuando yo esté allá” en Venezuela. “No quiero regresar”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-420000" name="module-420000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Y, sin embargo, el juez federal de inmigración asignado a escuchar su caso en el centro de Chicago no quedó convencido. Entre las dudas que citó al negar el caso: no podía creer que los dos agentes se subieran a una sola motocicleta junto con su víctima. Dijo que los documentos carecían de detalles cruciales y, ultimadamente, determinó que los policías, aunque uniformados, actuaban por un rencor personal y no por acciones oficiales.</p><p>El juez Matthew C. Beese, uno de los primeros de muchos nombramientos en la corte de inmigración de Chicago durante el segundo mandato del presidente Donald Trump, tiene ahora una de las tasas más bajas de aprobación de asilo en Chicago, contribuyendo a una tendencia nacional más amplia de tasas en pico.</p><p>En Chicago, la tasa de aprobación de asilo es apenas de 3.3% en lo que va del año; el año pasado fue de 14.6%. El promedio nacional cayó a 2.1%, comparado a 8.8%, según un análisis de Chicago Sun-Times y WBEZ de datos de la corte de inmigración.</p><p>Históricamente, el asilo ha sido una forma difícil de conseguir para quedarse en Estados Unidos, y exige pruebas de persecución en el país de origen que apunten específicamente a grupos protegidos de personas, como disidentes políticos o minorías étnicas.</p><p>Escapar de condiciones generales desesperadas, como la pobreza, la violencia o un gobierno fallido, nunca ha sido suficiente para obtener protección de asilo.</p><p>Desde enero de 2025, cuando el presidente recién inaugurado comenzó de inmediato a intensificar las deportaciones y a expulsar a millones de inmigrantes, su Departamento de Justicia (DOJ) ha impuesto una gran reorganización en la corte de inmigración que supervisa. Jueces veteranos con amplia experiencia como abogados de inmigración han sido desplazados y reemplazados por nuevos nombramientos. Una campaña nacional en redes sociales para reclutar nuevos jueces sigue presentando el cargo como un “juez de deportación”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>El Departamento de Justicia, que supervisa la corte de inmigración y a los jueces de inmigración, sigue anunciando vacantes en su sitio web para jueces “de deportación”.</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>En Chicago, muchos de los nuevos contratados antes trabajaban en derecho militar y administrativo, en lugar de derecho migratorio, y por eso llegan al estrado en gran medida sin el contexto importante sobre los países de origen de los inmigrantes que han huido.</p><p>Los jueces de inmigración también han quedado cargados de expedientes pesados, reglas más estrictas diseñadas para conceder menos casos de asilo y una nueva urgencia desde Washington, D.C. para cerrar casos de migrantes de ciertos países, dicen abogados y jueces recientemente destituidos.</p><p>También temen que el debido proceso en la corte de inmigración de Chicago se esté desvaneciendo.</p><p>“Cuando la gente habla de justicia en nuestro sistema migratorio, creo que la parte importante es si alguien ha tenido su día en corte”, dice Eva Saltzman, una de las juezas despedidas más recientemente, “y creo que si las personas reciben el debido proceso es un reflejo de la integridad del juez y de la integridad del gobierno en general”.</p><p>Al pedirle una entrevista, el Departamento de Justicia envió en cambio una declaración preparada por su oficina de prensa, en la que se negó a comentar sobre asuntos de personal.</p><p>“Reducir el rezago de la corte de inmigración sigue siendo una de las principales prioridades de esta administración. El Departamento de Justicia está restaurando la integridad de nuestro sistema migratorio al escuchar los casos de manera justa, expedita y uniforme, de conformidad con la ley”, decía.</p><p>“Este Departamento de Justicia sigue incorporando a talentosos profesionales de derecho comprometidos con proteger la seguridad nacional y la seguridad pública”.</p><h3>Sin experiencia en derecho migratorio</h3><p>Los jueces de inmigración de Chicago han visto una puerta giratoria durante la segunda administración de Trump. En medio de una avalancha de cambios del Departamento de Justicia, algunos jueces con experiencia aceptaron jubilaciones tempranas o renunciaron, pero al menos seis más, de una corte de unos 20, fueron despedidos sin explicación, dicen ellos.</p><p>Y de los 10 jueces nombrados recientemente para conocer casos en Chicago, siete parecen estar comenzando su práctica en derecho migratorio con este ascenso.</p><p>Una revisión de registros públicos muestra que esto también es cierto para el juez Beese, el juez del venezolano, quien fue nombrado el pasado octubre. Aunque es un abogado experimentado con licencia desde 2003, la biografía de Beese en el Departamento de Justicia indica que sus siete años como juez los pasó primero como juez municipal en una localidad de Oklahoma de unas 500 personas y luego como juez de derecho administrativo para la comisión reguladora estatal de Oklahoma que supervisa servicios públicos, petróleo y gas.</p><p>Como abogado, fue durante mucho tiempo fiscal adjunto de la ciudad de Muskogee, Oklahoma, y ejerció derecho de familia, penal y general cerca de Rockford, Illinois.</p><p>Otros nuevos contratados venían de carreras como jueces militares y como fiscales. Los tres que tienen experiencia en inmigración han trabajado para el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>Jennifer Peyton, exasistente del juez principal de la corte de inmigración de Chicago hasta que fue despedida en julio de 2025, dice que ahora se ha encontrado explicando aspectos del derecho migratorio a algunos de los nuevos jueces, ya que volvió a representar a inmigrantes en la práctica privada.</p><p>Dice que ha tenido audiencias con algunos de los jueces más nuevos, incluso en Chicago, en las que han dicho cosas contrarias al derecho migratorio. “Y yo digo, ‘eso es imposible por la situación de este caso, eso no puede pasar’”, dice Peyton. “Tuve suerte porque me enfoqué toda mi carrera en inmigración, así que ya tenía una comprensión bastante buena de [la ley de inmigración] desde el principio”.</p><p>Los nuevos jueces contratados desde 2025, en particular, están arrastrando hacia abajo la tasa de aprobación de asilo. De los 1,638 casos de asilo presentados ante ellos hasta agosto, solo han aprobado 25. Eso representa una tasa de aprobación de 1.5%.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-510000" name="html-embed-module-510000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-scatter" data-src="visualisation/30347671"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30347671/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="scatter visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Beese, por ejemplo, solo ha concedido 13 de los 802 casos que han pasado por su corte y ha negado 212. Ha declarado 511 de ellos “abandonados” —lo que podría significar que el inmigrante no se presentó a la corte o no cumplió requisitos como dejarse tomar las huellas dactilares o presentar pruebas—, lo que los coloca en camino a la deportación.</p><p>Dos de sus nuevos colegas, que entre ambos suman más de 500 resoluciones de asilo desde que fueron nombrados en mayo, aún no han concedido ninguna petición de asilo. Según sus biografías del Departamento de Justicia, ambos fueron fiscales y abogados de ICE: Shawn J. Abraham durante seis meses en Chicago y Jaime Poarch durante siete en Texas.</p><p>El análisis de Sun-Times/WBEZ utilizó datos publicados por la Oficina Ejecutiva de Revisión de Inmigración, como se llama la corte de inmigración para el gobierno, recopilados por el Deportation Data Project, hasta finales de agosto.</p><h3>Muchos cambios de reglas, muchos despidos</h3><p>Saltzman fue una de las dos juezas despedidas en julio, cuando los casos de asilo en Chicago alcanzaban su punto más alto. Una jueves en la tarde, mientras escuchaba casos, dice que le llegó a su bandeja de entrada un breve correo electrónico informándole que estaba despedida. Una jueza de inmigración desde 2016 y con evaluaciones de desempeño positivas, había sido asignada a casos de inmigrantes en centros de detención.</p><p>También sospecha que su nombramiento por la administración de Obama fue un motivo para su despido, y dijo en una entrevista, “he visto que quienes no fueron nombrados por esta administración fueron despedidos más rápidamente”.</p><div Luego vinieron los cambios de política sobre cómo los jueces podían decidir un caso de asilo, reduciendo los motivos que podían usar para declarar a una persona elegible o acelerando los plazos.</p><p>“Lo que sí vi, por supuesto, fueron muchas decisiones de la Junta de Apelaciones de Inmigración aclarando quién es elegible para diferentes formas de [asilo]”, dice Saltzman, “así que un caso que yo habría visto hace tres años, en el que parecía claro que esa persona había establecido su elegibilidad para asilo bajo los casos actuales publicados por la Junta de Apelaciones de Inmigración, esa persona ya no es elegible para asilo, y por eso me encontré, de acuerdo con la ley, resolviendo los casos de manera muy distinta a como lo habría hecho hace dos o tres años”.</p><p>A finales de junio, la jueza Elizabeth Treacy renunció bajo presión, diciendo que estaba abrumada por los casos y por cambios de reglas “incómodos”.</p><p>“De repente recibíamos correos electrónicos, y nunca se me dijo explícitamente por qué”, dice Treacy, “donde decía, ‘Bien, aquí está el número de casos; estos deben escucharse antes de tal fecha, deben completarse antes de tal fecha’, sin una explicación de por qué”.</p><p>Los somalíes, por ejemplo, que han sido atacados repetidamente por el presidente, de pronto vieron adelantarse sus fechas de audiencia, reduciendo su tiempo para reunir pruebas.</p><p>Los cambios le parecieron incorrectos a Treacy, quien trabajó en el lado de la aplicación de la ley migratoria durante ocho años y medio como abogada de ICE hasta 2019. entries.title: 'Goonie Gang' boss gets life in prison after reign of terror on Chicago's South Side
entries.summary: <p>On their way to kill<b> </b>a rival gang member 10 years ago, Romeo<b> </b>Blackman<b> </b>took a teenager under his wing and offered some words of encouragement from<b> </b>a leader in Englewood's “Goonie Boss”<b> </b>street gang, prosecutors said.</p><p>Blackman allegedly told the younger gang member to “make sure your shoelaces are tied tight” and to “tie the hood tight.”<b> </b></p><p>The boy then walked into a barbershop on May 26, 2016, opened fire —but missed the target, records show. He<b> </b>killed<b> </b>someone<b> </b>getting a haircut, instead.</p><p>“Blackman killed and ordered to kill without remorse,” prosecutors alleged. “The bodies and lives destroyed by Goonie rests upon his shoulder.”</p><p>Now,<b> </b>U.S. District Judge<b> </b>John Blakey has sentenced Blackman, 30, to life in prison, more than three years after a jury <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/7/5/23785059/leaders-of-goonie-gang-found-guilty-in-racketeering-case" target="_blank" >convicted<b> </b>Blackman<b> </b>and two others</a> of a racketeering conspiracy and held Blackman responsible for<b> </b>several murders, including the one in the barbershop in May 2016.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/22/23733615/goonie-boss-street-gang-members-trial-chicago-federal-courthouse-shattered-real-lives" target="_blank" >Goonie Boss gang members’ trial kicks off at Chicago federal courthouse, with prosecutor saying they ‘shattered real lives’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>While handing down the sentence Tuesday, Blakey said Blackman participated “not only in the taking of other people’s lives, but the corruption of young people.”</p><p>“The debt he owes to society is significant,” Blakey said.</p><p>Blackman’s life sentence was mandatory, and he appeared largely unmoved by the proceedings at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. At one point during the hearing, he leaned back in his chair and put his hands behind his head, elbows out, as a prosecutor detailed his murders.</p><p>When the judge asked Blackman if he had anything to say before the sentence was handed down, Blackman told him, “No, I’m OK.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </b>Smith<b> </b>and<b> </b>Jolicious<b> </b>Turman, at the end of a roughly seven-week trial. Smith<b> </b>and Turman are set to be sentenced in the coming months, with Smith also facing a mandatory life sentence.</p><p>Their hearings were delayed while the trio argued for acquittal<b> </b>or a new trial.<b> </b>Blackman’s attorneys encouraged Blakey to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/12/30/born-cocaine-goonie-gang-leader-life-sentence-killings" target="_blank" >hand down a lighter sentence</a>, calling the mandatory life term unconstitutional.</p><p>They also argued that Blackman was born<b> </b>with<b> </b>cocaine<b> </b>and<b> </b>alcohol<b> </b>in<b> </b>his<b> </b>system<b> </b>and grew up in a fractured home surrounded by violence.</p><p>Other victims of Blackman’s reign of terror included a man taking groceries<b> </b>out of his car who was apparently mistaken<b> </b>for a rival gang member, and a man who<b> </b>simply walked over to a car in which Blackman<b> </b>was a passenger<b> </b>in December 2015, prosecutors told the judge.</p><p>“Blackman got out of the vehicle and shot Andre Donner in the face,” they wrote, “killing him and sending a citizen running for his life.”</p><p>Blackman later “bragged that he FaceTimed”<b> </b>the man, a prosecutor told Blakey in court.</p><p>Trevante Reed, the young gang member who opened fire in the barbershop at Blackman’s direction, pleaded guilty in state court<b> </b>to the resulting murder of Gerald Sias<b> </b>and is now serving a 20-year prison sentence, records show.</p><p>Jurors also found Blackman responsible for the murders of Stanley<b> </b>Bobo<b> </b>on Oct. 23, 2014, and<b> </b>Krystal Jackson<b> </b>on Nov. 19, 2014.</p><p>But prosecutors say the damage went beyond those victims.</p><p>“There is also the Englewood community, the City of Chicago, and all those unnamed or unknown that were shot, killed, or scurried away while Goonie indiscriminately shot and terrorized others so they could become the toughest gang on the South Side of Chicago,” the feds wrote in a court filing.</p><p>“All of this was done under the guidance of Romeo Blackman, and he bears responsibility for those actions.”</p><div class="RelatedList entries.title: White Sox receive letter from their holiest fan, Pope Leo, before postseason opener
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> are in the Pope's thoughts and prayers, as well as "the Almighty's abundant blessings," as they begin the postseason.</p><p>So says Pope Leo XIV himself.</p><p>The pontiff and lifelong Sox fan sent a letter — on papal stationery and with the pope's seal imprinted — with well wishes for the team. The Sox said in a post on X that the letter arrived Tuesday at Rate Field.</p><p>"I was pleased to receive the kind letter that you sent following the game that took place at Rate Field on August 11, 2026," the pope wrote, referring to Pope Hat Night. "I am most grateful for this thoughtful gesture.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Earlier today, a letter from Pope Leo XIV arrived at Rate Field. Go White Sox! <a href="https://t.co/7qPKXPrDyz">pic.twitter.com/7qPKXPrDyz</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2105032478129815979?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>"As I have noted, 'sport can truly become a school of life, where all can learn that abundance does not come from victory at any cost, but from sharing, from respecting others and from the joy of walking together.' In this spirit, it is my hope that the White Sox will continue to foster bonds of friendship and solidarity among people, and thus bear hopeful witness to the possibility of living and working together in peace.</p><p>"With these sentiments, I willingly invoke the Almighty's abundant blessings upon you and your loved ones."</p><p>It wasn't exactly a pep talk for the playoffs because the letter was dated Sept. 9. But it arrived before Game 1 of the American League wild-card series, so maybe there is some divine intervention at work.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest
